sections.title: Selling Items Used for Worship; the Prohibition of Lifnei Iver
sections.html:
It is forbidden to cause a person to stumble into a transgression, whether a Jew or a gentile, as it is stated: "You shall not place a stumbling block before the blind; you shall fear your God, I am the Lord" (Vayikra 19:14). That is, just as it is forbidden to place before a blind person an obstacle that will injure his body, so it is forbidden to place before a person an obstacle that will cause him to stumble into a transgression that will injure his soul (Avoda Zara 6a; Ran ad loc.). Therefore, it is forbidden to sell a gentile items needed for idolatry, such as vessels used for worship or a white rooster, which they customarily sacrificed to idols. Even when the gentile does not say that he intends to sacrifice the rooster to an idol, as long as it is reasonable to assume that this is his intention, for example if he insists that it be white, it is forbidden to sell it to him (Avoda Zara 13b; SA YD 151:1).

Some say that even when the gentile can buy his items of worship from others, it is rabbinically forbidden to sell them to him, because the seller thereby assists him in committing a transgression. Others say that the prohibition of lifnei iver applies only when without the Jew the gentile would be unable to commit the transgression, but if he can buy his items of worship from another gentile, there is no prohibition for the Jew to sell them to him, since in any case the gentile will commit the transgression. In practice, in a time of need the custom is to be lenient, and those who are scrupulous try to avoid it (Rema YD 151:1).1

sections.title: The Prohibition of Lifnei Iver in Selling to Merchants
sections.html:
It is permitted to sell a gentile merchant large quantities of items for him to sell to other people who will likely use them for idolatry, such as roosters that they customarily sacrifice to idols. For the obligation placed upon us is not to cause the gentile before us to stumble, as it is stated: "You shall not place a stumbling block before the blind," but we bear no responsibility to ensure that the one who buys from us will not cause other gentiles to stumble; this is called lifnei de-lifnei ("before the one who is before") (Avoda Zara 14a; SA YD 151:1).

But when it is likely that the merchant who bought from us will thereby cause Jews to stumble, it is forbidden to sell to him, for the responsibility placed upon us toward our Jewish brethren is greater, and even lifnei de-lifnei is forbidden (Rosh; Taz 151:3). Therefore, it is forbidden to sell non-kosher foods to a merchant when one might mistakenly think that they are kosher and a Jew might stumble on them.2

sections.title: The Prohibition of Partnership with One Who Customarily Swears by His Idols
sections.html:
It is forbidden to cause a gentile to swear or vow in the name of idols, as it is stated: "Make no mention of the name of other gods; it shall not be heard through your mouth" (Shemot 23:13). "It shall not be heard through your mouth" means that one should also not cause others to swear by their idols. In order not to come to this prohibition, the Sages forbade entering into a partnership with an idolater, because such a partnership is based on an understanding that if they come to a dispute, the gentile will swear by his idols, and he will not lie, since he honours them (Sanhedrin 63b; SA ḤM 176:51).

However, when a monetary dispute has broken out between a Jew and an idolater, and only if the Jew demands that he swear might he admit the truth, according to many it is permitted for the Jew to demand that the gentile swear in order to try to save his money. For in a case of dispute, the prohibition of making him swear is rabbinic, and therefore in a pressing situation, to prevent a loss, it is permitted to make him swear. Others say that it is forbidden by Torah law to make him swear by his idols, and therefore even in a pressing situation it is forbidden to make him swear.3

sections.title: The Prohibition of Doing Business on Their Festival Days and Before Them
sections.html:
The Sages forbade doing business with an idolater on his eid (his festival day), because out of the sense of satisfaction at his success in business he will likely give thanks for it to his idol on his festival day, and it turns out that the Jew caused this and transgressed what is stated: "Make no mention of the name of other gods; it shall not be heard through your mouth" (Shemot 23:13). The Sages also forbade doing business with them during the three days before their festival, because on those days they used to prepare the sacrifices they offered to the idol on the festival day, and any success that came their way on those days they believed came to them by virtue of the idol, which looked favourably upon the sacrifice they were preparing for it, and therefore they gave thanks to it for this. But four days before their festival they did not usually prepare the festival sacrifice, and therefore there is no concern that the idolater will connect his success with his acts of worship.

Included in the prohibition of doing business are selling or buying, lending or borrowing an object, lending or borrowing money, and collecting a loan or repaying it, for each of these activities can arouse a sense of satisfaction in the idolater, and if it takes place on his festival day, or on the days in which he prepares his worship for his festival day, he will likely give thanks for it to his idol.4

sections.title: The Permission in Practice
sections.html:
The Sages ruled that outside the Land of Israel it is permitted to do business with idolaters during the three days before their festival, and only on their festival day itself is it forbidden (Avoda Zara 11b). This is because the Sages saw that idolaters had become less devout, and less careful to give thanks to the idols for their successes. Similarly, we learned (Ḥullin 13a-b) that when idolaters used to have in mind, when slaughtering an animal, that the slaughter was for their idols, there were Sages who ruled that all meat slaughtered by an idolater is forbidden for any benefit, like the law of an "offering to idolatry" (above 10:2). However, Rabbi Yoḥanan said that this law does not apply outside the Land, because "gentiles outside the Land are not idolaters; rather, they are following the custom of their ancestors," and therefore they do not have the idols in mind when they slaughter, and consequently the meat they slaughtered is permitted for benefit.

In addition, after the destruction of the Second Temple, Israel was scattered among the nations and became dependent on them, and there was concern that if they did not do business with them for many days, they would lose their source of livelihood, and hostility toward them would also increase. Therefore, they were lenient to do business with them during the three days before their festival. Later, when the Jewish community in the Land weakened, in the Land too the custom was to be lenient during the three days before their festival. In addition, over the years the custom of sacrificing animals to idols declined, and consequently they were not occupied with preparing sacrifices during the three days before their festival, and the concern that they would attribute their success on those three days to the help of the idols diminished.

And although, in principle, on the basis of the reasons for permission mentioned above it would have been possible to permit doing business even on their festival day, they continued to forbid it, because refraining from business on their festival day alone did not greatly harm livelihood and was not dangerous on account of hostility.

Over the years, the economic need to do business even on their festival days kept growing. The danger of hostility also grew. At the same time, the idolaters became less devout toward their idols, and many used to associate the Name of Heaven in their thanksgiving, as the Christians did. Therefore, already in the days of the Geonim they ruled leniently to do business with them even on their festival day, and this is the halakha (SA YD 148:12).5

sections.title: The Prohibition of Benefiting Idolatry
sections.html:
It is forbidden to buy at a fair that was held on the days of an idolatrous festival, at which a tax was paid to the idolatry from every purchase, because it is forbidden to give benefit to idolatry. If one transgressed and bought, the Sages penalised him so that he loses what he bought: if he bought an animal, he must cut off its hooves from the knee joint downward, so that it will be evident that it is forbidden to benefit from it; if he bought garments, he must leave them to rot; if he bought metal vessels, he must throw them into the Dead Sea (Avoda Zara 13a; SA YD 149:3).

However, it is permitted to take part in a fair at which the regional trade took place, even if it is held on an idolatrous festival day, since its main purpose is general commerce and not worship, and also they did not customarily pay a tax from it to the idolatry. Most fairs in the period of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim were conducted in this way (Rema YD 149:4).

One whose house was adjacent to a house of idolatry, and the wall between them fell, it is forbidden for him, as a Jew, to rebuild it, because by doing so he also builds the wall of the house of idolatry, and thus gives benefit to it. Rather, he should move back four amot and build the wall of his house, so that they will not be able to use his wall as a wall for themselves. And so that they will not be able to benefit from the space between his house and the house of idolatry, he should use those four amot for a lavatory or other degrading things, so that no benefit will accrue to them from it (Avoda Zara 47a-b).6

Likewise, it is forbidden to sell land for a house of idolatry to be built on it, because by doing so one gives benefit to idolatry and also assists in its construction. When there is a great need, it is permitted outside the Land to sell the land to a gentile broker, who will sell the land to whomever he wishes.7

sections.title: Using Property Belonging to Idolatry
sections.html:
If a house of idolatry had a bathhouse, a museum, apartments or shops for rent: if the payment they collect is designated for the needs of the idolatry itself, it is forbidden to pay them, because of the prohibition of giving benefit to idolatry. But if the payment is designated for the needs of the community associated with that idolatry, it is permitted to enter there for payment. Likewise, it is permitted to enter there free of charge when there is no need to thank the priests for the entry.

If the payment is designated for the upkeep of the priests: if the building one is paying for is adjacent to the house of idolatry, it is forbidden to pay, since it appears that the payment goes to the idolatry itself (Avoda Zara 51b; SA YD 143:3, 5). But if the building is far from the house of idolatry, then even when the payment goes to the upkeep of the priests it is permitted to pay them, since it does not appear to be giving benefit to the idolatry itself (Rema YD 143:3).8

If a bathhouse was the private property of a priest of idolatry, it is permitted to pay him in order to bathe, since this fee is considered his personal profit and not a payment for the maintenance of the idolatry or its worship (Rashba 51b, and Ritva in the name of Rabbeinu Yona). Similarly, it is permitted to rent from a priest a shop or an apartment that belongs to him.

It is forbidden to insure idols, or even their accessories and ornaments, because they are forbidden for benefit, and by receiving insurance premiums for them one benefits from their existence (see Avoda Zara 63b; SA YD 133:6). If the person requesting the insurance is a decent gentile whom it would not be right to offend, or when there is concern about hostility, one should mediate between him and a gentile who will insure him, and take care not to receive a commission for the mediation (see Har Tzvi YD 117).

sections.title: Building and Repairs in a House of Idolatry
sections.html:
In addition to the Torah prohibition against making an image for idolatry (above 3:3), it is also forbidden to build something that serves idolatry or to add ornamentation to it. Therefore, it is forbidden to build a platform on which an idolatrous image is placed; likewise it is forbidden to build a room or hall in which idolatry is placed, and likewise it is forbidden to install its windows, both because they serve as a shelter for the idolatry and because they are an ornament to it. Likewise, it is forbidden for a Jewish contractor to carry out these works through his gentile workers, since they carry out the work at his instruction. But it is permitted for a Jew to build the rooms and entrance halls in front of the hall in which the idolatry stands, and likewise it is permitted to decorate them, since they are tashmish de-tashmish (an accessory of an accessory) and noy de-noy (an ornament of an ornament). Since Christianity is idolatry for Jews, a church is included in this as well: the place where they bow to the cross is tashmish avoda zara (an accessory of idolatry), and the other rooms are tashmish de-tashmish (SA YD 143:2; Shakh 1).

After the house of idolatry has already been built, it is forbidden to enter it even to make repairs to a tashmish de-tashmish, because one who enters there appears to be entering for worship. But if he is dressed as a workman and comes with another Jewish worker, there is no suspicion, and he may carry out repairs in rooms that are not used for worship (see Maharsham 3:72). However, ideally it is better for a Jew to keep away even from building or renovating a tashmish de-tashmish or noy de-noy of idolatry.9

sections.title: Renting a House to an Idolater
sections.html:
The Sages forbade renting a dwelling to an idolater, because he customarily sets up an idolatrous image in his house, and they based their words on what is stated: "You shall not bring an abomination into your house" (Devarim 7:26). That is, the Torah prohibition is that a Jew should bring idolatry into his house, and the Sages added and forbade renting a house to a gentile who customarily sets up an idolatrous image in his house; but they did not forbid renting to one who occasionally brings it into his house on a temporary basis (Mishna Avoda Zara 21a; Tosafot, s.v. "Af"; SA YD 151:10).

There is no prohibition against hosting in one's home a Christian who wears a cross around his neck, for the main halakhic view is that it is a symbol and not an image that is worshipped (below 12:12).

When there is a need for the help of a Christian or Hindu "foreign worker" who will live in one of the rooms of the house and care for an elderly person or a patient requiring nursing care, one should agree with him that he will not bring into his room a cross or a Hindu statuette in order to bow to it. In a pressing situation, when it is not possible to agree on this and there is no choice but to rely on his help, one should rent the room to him, and he should remove the mezuza from it until the end of the period in which he lives in the house.10
